title: Governor Newsom statement on compromise to address wildfire risk, support fire survivors, and create stronger accountability
key_claim: The three-party compromise on Senate Bill 492 blocks hedge funds from buying wildfire survivor claims, bars utility executive bonuses when the company ignites a fire and speeds survivor payments, but the Governor states the system needs full reform and urges the Legislature to return next year to secure the Wildfire Fund's long-term durability and stabilise electricity rates.
frame_summary: The Governor is arguing that the enacted compromise is deliberately partial, and that the item left unresolved is the financial durability of the Wildfire Fund and utilities' access to low-cost capital rather than the mechanics of compensating survivors.
verbatim_quote: It also establishes a Statewide Community Wildfire Strategy to better coordinate prevention and preparedness efforts across the state.
verbatim_list: We reached a compromise that blocks hedge funds from profiteering off wildfire survivors, bars utility executives from taking bonuses when their company ignites a fire, and gets money into survivors’ hands faster.
notes: Primary record of what the 29 August 2026 California compromise did and did not contain. The Governor's own framing concedes the liability rule was left untouched.

title: PUC Approves Wildfire Mitigation Plans for Idaho Power, Pacific Power, and PGE
key_claim: On 29 June 2026 the Oregon Public Utility Commission approved the 2026-2028 wildfire mitigation plans for Idaho Power, Portland General Electric and Pacific Power, and simultaneously adopted staff recommendations for greater transparency, stronger modelling practices and further demonstration of cost-effective mitigation investment.
frame_summary: The Oregon regulator is arguing that plan approval is an active supervisory instrument delivering safer communities, while its own attached conditions concede that cost-effectiveness has not yet been demonstrated at the point of approval.
verbatim_quote: The Oregon Public Utility Commission (PUC) today approved the 2026–2028 Wildfire Mitigation Plans for Idaho Power (UM 2209), Portland General Electric (UM 2208), and Pacific Power (UM 2207).
verbatim_list: The Commission also adopted the PUC staff recommendations for additional improvement across the utilities’ programs to support greater transparency, stronger modeling practices, and further demonstration of cost-effective mitigation investments.

The wildfire mitigation plans are required under Senate Bill 762 (2021), which directs electric utilities in Oregon to identify areas of heightened wildfire risk within their service territories, develop measures to reduce ignition risks, and outline PSPS protocols during dangerous conditions.
notes: Oregon state newsroom carrying the Oregon PUC announcement. Used as the dated, primary record that the plan-approval machinery is operating at scale in the current cycle.

title: Northwest Utilities' Wildfire Risk and Spending Is Skyrocketing
key_claim: Northwest investor-owned utilities forecast more than doubling annual wildfire mitigation budgets from $279 million in 2023 to $711 million in 2028 while championing liability shields keyed to compliance with their own regulator-approved mitigation plans; Idaho and Montana enacted such laws in 2025, Montana's barring a court from weighing a utility's actual incremental cost, and credit rating agencies still assess every Northwest investor-owned utility as stable and investment grade with the exception of PacifiCorp.
frame_summary: Sightline is arguing that plan-compliance liability shields are premature and structurally unsound, because state regulators lack the expertise and staffing to test the plans the shields rest on, and the shields therefore reward capital overspending rather than measurable risk reduction.
verbatim_quote: The laws that utilities are pushing limit liability based on the extent to which a company follows its own, regulator-approved wildfire mitigation plan.
verbatim_list: Between 2023 and 2028, Northwest IOUs forecast more than doubling their annual wildfire mitigation budgets, from $279 million to $711 million.
Roughly 12 percent of IOUs’ power lines are strung in fire-risky places, according to Sightline’s review of utilities’ most recent wildfire mitigation plans.
Montana’s law is especially generous, barring a court from considering a utility’s “actual incremental cost” in weighing whether it followed its approved plans.
However, credit rating agencies continue to assess all other Northwest IOUs’ outlook as “stable.”

“Even in California, we had 80 people working on these, and we felt fairly outgunned [by the utility]. The government does not have the level of expertise to do the scrutiny that’s needed,” said Melissa Semcer, former Deputy Director of California’s Office of Energy Infrastructure Safety, the body responsible for monitoring utility wildfire mitigation plans.
notes: The analytical spine for the multi-state mechanism and the principal counter-evidence source: Sightline argues the shields are premature because ratings remain stable everywhere except PacifiCorp.

publisher: Energy Institute Blog, Energy Institute at Haas, University of California, Berkeley
title: Who Should Pay for Utility-Ignited Wildfires?
key_claim: California's inverse-condemnation strict-liability doctrine lets property owners recover damages and legal fees whether or not the utility was negligent, which concentrates incentives on the narrow set of ignition risks utilities control while leaving home hardening, fuel treatment and land-use decisions under-incentivised; limiting utility liability to controllable risks could produce more effective and more affordable risk reduction.
frame_summary: The Energy Institute is arguing that wildfire liability allocation should be treated as an incentive-design question rather than a fairness contest, and that the current rule mis-targets mitigation spending toward the utility system and away from cheaper community-level measures.
verbatim_quote: But that liability should be limited to the risks they can actually control.
verbatim_list: Over 28 days, the Eaton Fire killed 19 people and destroyed nearly 9,500 structures.
In California, a doctrine called “inverse condemnation” allows property owners to recover property damages and legal fees whether or not the utility is found negligent.
notes: Named-author research blog of a university energy research institute; classified Tier 2 as academic-institution synthesis work rather than an individual commentator's blog.

title: Newsom makes last-minute push to help California utilities facing wildfire bills
key_claim: California's $21 billion Wildfire Fund, capitalised half by utility shareholders and half by a $2.50 monthly customer surcharge, is expected to be drained by Eaton Fire claims, and the Governor's package proposed limiting or eliminating insurers' subrogation right to recoup wildfire payouts from utilities.
frame_summary: CalMatters is arguing that the wildfire package is fundamentally a contest over which balance sheet absorbs climate-driven fire loss, with utilities, insurers, ratepayers and survivors each manoeuvring to avoid ending up as the residual holder.
verbatim_quote: The state wildfire fund is expected to be drained once the costs of insurance claims, Edison’s multimillion-dollar voluntary settlements with survivors and numerous unsettled lawsuits are tallied.
verbatim_list: The state created a $21 billion wildfire fund, paid for half by utility shareholders and half by customers through a $2.50 surcharge on their monthly electricity bills, to pay victims’ claims, provided the utilities follow stricter safety regulations.
Newsom is proposing to limit — or eliminate entirely — insurance companies’ right to recoup money from utilities when a utility-caused fire forces those insurers to pay out homeowners’ claims.
notes: Used for the subrogation mechanism and the Wildfire Fund's exhaustion path. Nonprofit newsroom; positional only in that it reports the competing industry claims rather than adjudicating them.

title: Edison CEO: California utilities face credit downgrades without wildfire reforms
key_claim: Edison International's chief executive told analysts on 30 July 2026 that Southern California Edison is rated BBB- by S&P with no room left inside investment grade, and warned that failure to enact a credit-supportive wildfire framework before the 31 August session close would raise the cost of debt passed through to customers; SCE had committed about $1.6 billion to fire victims and faced more than 2,000 Eaton Fire lawsuits with 32,000 plaintiffs as of 23 July.
frame_summary: Utility Dive is arguing that the operative constraint from wildfire liability has become the utility's credit rating and cost of debt rather than its near-term solvency, which relocates the policy question from victim compensation to capital-market access.
verbatim_quote: If you look at just the S&P ratings, it's BBB- for [SCE]. So there's nowhere to go in investment grade, right? The next step is non-investment grade.
verbatim_list: According to the company's quarterly filings, SCE has committed some $1.6 billion to fire victims via two settlements with insurance companies and through its Wildfire Recovery Compensation Program.
As of July 23, SCE was named in more than 2,000 lawsuits, with 32,000 individual plaintiffs, related to the Eaton Fire.
In April, the California Public Utilities Commission granted a request by SCE to collect an additional $274 million to $650 million from customers this year to cover Eaton Fire costs.
notes: Trade press carrying a verbatim earnings-call quotation from the Edison International CEO. Cited for the rating-floor claim, which is the financial transmission mechanism the scan rests on.
